21 Which statement about longitudinal waves and transverse waves is not correct?
A
Both waves can be polarised.
B
Both waves can form stationary waves.
C
Both waves can transfer energy as progressive waves.
D
Both waves obey the equation v = fλ.

hints: Notice the question asks for the statement that is not correct, so test each statement for both longitudinal oscillations parallel to travel and transverse oscillations perpendicular to travel.
Recall that polarisation means isolating oscillations to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
Check whether stationary wave formation, energy transfer by a progressive wave, and $v = f\lambda$ depend on the oscillation direction or apply to all progressive waves.
walkthrough: Identify the vibration directions: in a transverse wave oscillations are perpendicular to propagation, in a longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel to propagation.
State the rule for polarisation: it passes vibrations in only one plane perpendicular to propagation, so it requires a choice of perpendicular directions.

Apply this to the two types: a transverse wave has many possible perpendicular planes so it can be polarised, but a longitudinal wave has only one line of vibration along propagation so it cannot be polarised.
Check the other properties: both types can superpose to form stationary waves, both can travel as progressive waves carrying energy, and both satisfy $v = f\lambda$.
Therefore the claim that both waves can be polarised is the not correct statement. This is option A

A.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised because polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane perpendicular to travel, which is impossible for longitudinal oscillations along travel.

B.explanation: Both types can form stationary waves by superposition of two progressive waves of the same type travelling in opposite directions.

C.explanation: Both types can be progressive waves that transfer energy from source to absorber in the direction of propagation.

D.explanation: Both types obey $v = f\lambda$ where $v$ is wave speed, $f$ is frequency and $\lambda$ is wavelength.
